Question: How can AI tools help students develop lateral thinking and creative problem-solving skills?
Answer: In the case of lateral thinking, not at all. AI (as it is today, in 2024) is the very definition of brute force thinking; the opposite of lateral thinking. “Creative problem-solving” is a pleonasm but aside from that, is also an excellent example of a skill that current AI is not able to acquire. However, there are problems that can be solved through targeted use of AI. I suspect, however that this use of AI as a tool or component of the system requires a solid base in problem-solving and would not therefore teach you much about it

Question: Why do Romance languages assign genders for inanimate objects?
Answer: They don't. The genders of the words for inanimate objects are not assigned, they are acquired through the course of linguistic history. When neologism occurs, gender is usually chosen either by strict rules (in French, for instance, if a new word’s main root is Greek or seems Greek-ish, the word will be masculine), or because the word resembles existing words, and the gender conforms.

Question: Does a story still count as fiction if it is a memoir based on something that actually happened?
Answer: “Fiction” literally means “made up, invented,” “memoir” literally means “what you can remember.” Delightfully, this means a memoir can be untrue without being fiction, if your memory of events is “unreliable.” Good stories based on real events are often called a “fictionalized account.” There are numerous flavours of this: Last year there was a biopic of Robert Oppenheimer. It presents certain events of his life told as a story through the medium of film. It's mostly not fiction. James Cameron's Titanic is pretty factual when it comes to the ship and what befell it. However, Rose and Jack are completely fictional. This is a mixture of “cinematic fact” and pure fiction. In Moby Dick, the vast majority of the detail of life on a whaling ship is authentic and accurate; Melville had been on the crew of a whaling ship. The rest of the story is made up. In 20 000 Leagues Beneath the Seas, Pierre Arronax is a passenger in a submarine all around the world. Of course, at the time of writing no such vessel existed. However, the geography, oceanography and the (extensive) lists of fish were correct and accurate to the extent of knowledge at the time of writing. The Australian comedian Clive James called his autobiography “Unreliable Memoirs.” The places he described were all real, and many of the people, too. Most of the events probably really happened. But the stories are very funny to read, so it is fair to suppose that James alliwed himself some license; nonetheless, “Unreliable Memoirs” is not usually considered to be fiction. I hope that helps.

Question: What adjustments would you make to your nation's educational policies if you had the power to do so in order to raise standards across the board?
Answer: Here in France secondary education is profoundly broken. It is Ministry of Education policy that every year a specific percentage of French high school (lycee) students will obtain their baccalaureat (“bac”) - our “equivalent” to a HS Diploma or A-Levels. Because each school must meet the statistics, every year, after children have sat their exams, schools convene a board where they examine the individual cases of those who did not get the required scores to receive their Bac and they “adjust” some of the scores according to “mitigating arguments” given by teachers. This, obviously is a symptom of a broken system but very few people will admit to what this really implies: That the Bac itself is meaningless. Yet, most admissions to university are based on your Bac scores (sometimes combined with your final year report cards). Add to this the fact that most University courses have a continuous dropout and fail rate - a third give up before completing their degree; most during their first year and a proportion of those subsequently attempt a different degree but most do not. This, might or might not be a symptom of a broken system but it too shows that the Bac itself is meaningless. AS IS MOST EVALUATION DURING SCHOOL. The purpose of testing pupils is 100% political: it’s for moronic politicians who can’t grasp the basics of education, but also it’s for moronic voters who think that a good education is one where it’s easy to measure what you know. For information, it isn’t. A n adult who is the product of a good education comes out of it with ONE MAJOR SKILL: the ability to learn. A good education teaches you how to learn. Which is why what you know when you are 18 is utterly irrelevant. There is NOTHING that you need to know for any University degree course that, at age 19/20 or so, you cannot learn in under a year, if your schooling has taught you how to learn. The what is of no importance.
